title: Logic: The Syllogism and the Laws of Thought
subtitle: How Aristotle invented a science of good reasoning, almost from nothing
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what a categorical syllogism is and identify its premises, conclusion and three terms.
By the end you will be able to recognize the four kinds of categorical statement (A, E, I, O) and test simple syllogisms for validity.
By the end you will be able to distinguish validity from truth and explain what makes an argument sound.
By the end you will be able to state the law of non-contradiction and the law of excluded middle and explain why Aristotle thought the first is the firmest principle of all.
By the end you will be able to explain the difference between deduction and induction and why both matter.
hook:
Here is an argument. All cats are mammals. All mammals breathe air. Therefore all cats breathe air. Obviously fine. Now here is another. All cats are mammals. All dogs are mammals. Therefore all cats are dogs. Obviously wrong. But here is the strange question: *what exactly* is the difference? Both have two true starting points. Both sound confident. Why does one force its conclusion on you and the other not?

For most of human history, nobody had a systematic answer. People argued, persuaded, and caught each other in contradictions, as Socrates did in the marketplace (Day 9) and the Sophists did in the law courts (Day 8). But nobody had worked out the general rules that separate good reasoning from bad, the way a grammar separates correct sentences from broken ones. Aristotle did. At the end of one of his works, he remarks that on this subject he found nothing already worked out to build on. Today we look at the tool he built, which philosophers used for over two thousand years.

sections.heading: The Organon: A Toolkit for Thinking
sections.body:
**Logic** is the study of reasoning: specifically, of which conclusions really follow from which starting points. The word comes from the Greek *logos*, which we met with Heraclitus on Day 4 and which can mean word, speech, reason or account. Aristotle himself called his subject ‘analytics’, but later followers grouped his logical works together under the name **Organon**, meaning ‘tool’ or ‘instrument’. The name says something important. For the Peripatetics (Day 16), logic was not one branch of knowledge among others. It was the instrument you needed before you could do any of them properly.

The Organon includes six works:

- *Categories*: the basic kinds of things we can say about something (substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time and others).
- *On Interpretation*: how statements are built, and how they can be true or false.
- *Prior Analytics*: the theory of the syllogism, the heart of today's lesson.
- *Posterior Analytics*: how syllogisms are used to build scientific knowledge.
- *Topics*: techniques for debate and arguing from commonly accepted opinions.
- *Sophistical Refutations*: a catalogue of **fallacies**, arguments that look valid but are not, of the kind the Sophists used to trap opponents.

Why did this happen in Athens in the fourth century BCE? Think of the setting. Athens was a city of law courts, assemblies and philosophical schools where arguments decided life and death. Plato's Academy taught dialectic and geometry, and geometry already showed how conclusions could be proved step by step from definitions and axioms. Aristotle asked what *all* good proofs have in common, whatever their subject. That move, from studying particular arguments to studying the *form* of arguments, is the birth of logic.

sections.heading: The Syllogism: Two Premises and a Conclusion
sections.body:
Aristotle defined a **syllogism** (Greek *syllogismos*, ‘reckoning together’) very broadly as an argument in which, certain things being stated, something else follows of necessity because of them. In practice, his theory concerns a specific kind, the **categorical syllogism**, built from three statements:

> All humans are mortal.
> All Greeks are humans.
> Therefore, all Greeks are mortal.

The first two statements are the **premises**, the starting points we accept. The last is the **conclusion**, what follows from them. (The famous textbook example about Socrates being mortal, by the way, is not in Aristotle; it comes from later teachers, and strictly speaking it uses an individual name, which Aristotle's system does not quite handle.)

Every categorical syllogism contains exactly three **terms**, the general words that name groups of things. In our example they are ‘humans’, ‘mortal’ and ‘Greeks’.

- The **major term** is the predicate of the conclusion (‘mortal’).
- The **minor term** is the subject of the conclusion (‘Greeks’).
- The **middle term** appears in both premises but never in the conclusion (‘humans’). It is the bridge that links the other two.

The middle term is the secret of the whole thing. The premises connect Greeks to humans and humans to mortality, so the conclusion can connect Greeks directly to mortality. If there is no proper bridge, the argument collapses. That is exactly what went wrong with the cats and dogs in our hook: ‘mammals’ appears in both premises, but in a way that does not link cats to dogs at all. Both are inside the mammal circle, but that does not put either inside the other.

A helpful way to picture this, though it was invented much later, is with circles. Draw a big circle for mortal things, a smaller one inside it for humans, and a smaller one inside that for Greeks. You can see the conclusion at a glance: the Greek circle is inside the mortal circle.

sections.heading: Four Kinds of Statement and the Valid Forms
sections.body:
Aristotle noticed that the statements used in syllogisms come in just four basic kinds. They differ in **quantity** (all or some) and **quality** (affirming or denying). Medieval logicians gave them letter names, from the Latin words *affirmo* (I affirm) and *nego* (I deny), which are still used today:

- **A** (universal affirmative): All S are P. ‘All whales are mammals.’
- **E** (universal negative): No S are P. ‘No whales are fish.’
- **I** (particular affirmative): Some S are P. ‘Some mammals are whales.’
- **O** (particular negative): Some S are not P. ‘Some mammals are not whales.’

These four statements are related in a neat pattern. An A statement and an O statement with the same terms **contradict** each other: exactly one must be true. If ‘All swans are white’ is false, then ‘Some swans are not white’ must be true, and vice versa. The same goes for E and I.

By combining these four kinds of statement and arranging the middle term in different positions (Aristotle called these arrangements **figures**), you can generate many possible syllogisms. Aristotle worked through them systematically and showed which are **valid** and which are not. Medieval students memorized the valid forms using made-up Latin names in which the vowels give the statement types. The most famous is **Barbara** (A, A, A):

> All mammals are animals.
> All dogs are mammals.
> Therefore, all dogs are animals.

Another is **Celarent** (E, A, E): No reptiles are mammals; all snakes are reptiles; therefore no snakes are mammals.

Aristotle also gave rules of thumb for spotting invalid forms. Two negative premises never yield a conclusion (‘No cats are dogs; no dogs are fish’ tells you nothing about cats and fish). And the middle term must cover its whole class in at least one premise, which is why the cats and dogs argument fails: neither premise says anything about *all* mammals.

The astonishing thing is that the subject matter does not matter. You can replace dogs and mammals with stars, numbers or virtues, and Barbara stays valid. Validity depends on the *form* of the argument, not its content. That insight is the foundation of all formal logic, from Aristotle to the computer you are reading this on.

sections.heading: Validity, Truth and Soundness
sections.body:
Here is the most important lesson in all of elementary logic, and one that trips up beginners again and again: **validity is not the same as truth**.

An argument is **valid** if its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises: *if* the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. Truth and falsity belong to individual statements; validity belongs to the connection between them.

This means a valid argument can have a false conclusion:

> All fish can fly.
> All sharks are fish.
> Therefore, all sharks can fly.

This is Barbara, and it is perfectly valid. The conclusion is false only because the first premise is false. Logic did its job: it told you that *if* fish fly, sharks do. Garbage in, garbage out.

And an invalid argument can have a true conclusion:

> All dogs are animals.
> All cats are animals.
> Therefore, all cats are mammals.

Every statement here is true, but the conclusion does not follow from the premises; it just happens to be true for other reasons.

So philosophers use one more word. An argument is **sound** when it is valid *and* all its premises are true. A sound argument guarantees a true conclusion. This gives you two different ways to attack any argument, which is a handy everyday tool. You can deny a premise (‘that is not actually true’), or you can deny the connection (‘even if that were true, it would not follow’). Much confusion in public debate comes from mixing these up, for instance by assuming that because someone's conclusion is true, their reasoning must have been good.

sections.heading: The Laws of Thought: Non-Contradiction and Excluded Middle
sections.body:
Underneath the syllogism lie even more basic principles. Later logicians called them the **laws of thought**. The name is not Aristotle's, but the two most important principles are discussed by him, in Book IV (Gamma) of the *Metaphysics*.

The first is the **law of non-contradiction**. In Aristotle's words, it is impossible for the same thing to belong and not to belong at the same time to the same thing and in the same respect. Put simply: a statement and its denial cannot both be true. Your coffee cannot be both hot and not hot, at the same time, in the same part of the cup, in the same sense of ‘hot’. Those qualifications matter. A person can be tall compared to a child and short compared to a basketball player without contradiction. Remember Heraclitus' unity of opposites (Day 4): the road up and the road down are the same road, but described from different directions.

Aristotle calls this **the firmest of all principles**. Can he prove it? No, and he says so. Any proof would have to assume it. Asking for a proof of everything shows a lack of education, he says, since some things must be known without proof or the chain would go on forever. But he can show that anyone who denies it refutes himself. If an opponent says anything meaningful at all, say the word ‘human’, he means *this* and not *not-this*. The moment he speaks, he relies on the principle. Someone who truly rejected it, Aristotle jokes, would be no better than a plant. And why, he asks, does such a person walk to Megara rather than staying home, and not walk into a well? His actions show he believes some things really are better than others.

The second principle is the **law of excluded middle**: for any statement, either it or its denial is true; there is no third option in between. Either it is raining in Paris right now, or it is not. Some textbooks add a third law, the **law of identity** (a thing is itself, A is A), but this formulation comes from much later logicians.

These laws seem obvious, almost too obvious to state. But Aristotle was arguing against real opponents. Some followers of Heraclitus apparently thought that since everything is changing, nothing can be truly said; one, Cratylus, supposedly ended up just wagging his finger. And Protagoras' relativism (Day 8), if every appearance is true for whoever has it, seemed to make contradictory statements both true. Non-contradiction was Aristotle's line in the sand against both.

sections.heading: Deduction and Induction: Two Roads to Knowledge
sections.body:
A syllogism is a form of **deduction**: reasoning from general premises to a conclusion that follows necessarily. Deduction is powerful because it is airtight. But it has a limitation. It can only unpack what is already contained in the premises. Where do the premises come from?

Aristotle's answer is **induction** (Greek *epagoge*, ‘leading on’). Induction is reasoning from particular cases to a general rule. You notice that this skilled pilot is the best pilot, and this skilled charioteer is the best charioteer, and conclude that, in general, the skilled person is the best at their task (this is close to one of Aristotle's own examples). Induction is how science gathers its starting points: by observing many animals, Aristotle learns what is generally true of animals (Day 19).

Induction is not airtight. However many white swans you see, the next one could be black, as Europeans learned when they reached Australia. Aristotle knew induction gives a different kind of certainty from deduction. In the *Posterior Analytics*, he argues that perception, memory and experience build up until the mind (*nous*) grasps the universal principle. He compares this to a rout in battle: one soldier makes a stand, then another, until order is restored. The scientific ideal, for Aristotle, is to start from first principles grasped this way and then deduce the rest, like a geometry textbook.

The relationship between these two roads will become one of the great themes of this course. Medieval thinkers built huge structures of deduction on Aristotle's foundations. Francis Bacon (Day 41) attacked the syllogism as sterile and demanded a new induction. David Hume (Day 49) asked the devastating question of what justifies induction at all.

How good was Aristotle's logic? Extraordinarily good. Over two thousand years later, Immanuel Kant (Day 55) remarked that logic had not been able to take a single step forward since Aristotle and seemed complete. Kant was wrong, as it happens. The Stoics had already developed a logic of whole propositions (‘if... then’, ‘either... or’) that Aristotle's system lacked (Day 25), and in 1879 Gottlob Frege (Day 69) invented modern logic, which can handle statements about relations and individuals that syllogisms cannot express. But every logic student today still begins where Aristotle began: with the difference between what is true and what follows.

keyQuote.text: It is impossible for the same thing at the same time to belong and not to belong to the same thing and in the same respect.
keyQuote.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics IV (Gamma).3, 1005b19–20 (trans. W. D. Ross, adapted)

modernConnection.title: From Barbara to Bits: Logic in Your Pocket and Your Feed
modernConnection.body:
Every time you use a phone, you are relying on a descendant of Aristotle's insight that reasoning can be done by form alone. In 1854 the English mathematician George Boole published a book with a title borrowed straight from this tradition: *An Investigation of the Laws of Thought*. Boole showed that logical relations could be written as algebra, with 1 for true and 0 for false. In 1937 the American engineer Claude Shannon showed that Boole's algebra could describe electrical switching circuits. Today's computer chips contain billions of tiny switches performing logical operations like AND, OR and NOT. Your device does not understand dogs or mammals, which is exactly the point: like a syllogism, it processes form, not content.

Logic also matters in a more human way. Online arguments are full of the two mistakes this lesson warns against. People share articles whose conclusions they like without checking whether the reasoning holds, treating a true conclusion as proof of good argument. Others use perfectly valid reasoning from false premises, building elaborate conspiracy theories in which every step follows from the last but the starting point is invented. Asking two questions, ‘Are the premises true?’ and ‘Does the conclusion really follow?’, is one of the simplest and most powerful habits of critical thinking.

The comparison has limits. Real-world reasoning is rarely a neat syllogism. Most of what we believe comes from induction, probability, testimony and judgment, which Aristotle's formal logic does not capture well. Modern AI systems, interestingly, mostly learn by something closer to induction from vast data than by deduction from rules, which is one reason they can sound fluent yet contradict themselves. Aristotle would not be surprised. He thought both roads, deduction and induction, were needed, and that the law of non-contradiction was the first test any thinker, human or machine, must pass.

vocabulary.definition: The study of reasoning, especially of which conclusions follow from which premises, regardless of subject matter.
vocabulary.example: Aristotle's logic shows that the same valid form works whether we are talking about animals, numbers or stars.

vocabulary.definition: An argument in which a conclusion follows necessarily from premises; in Aristotle's categorical syllogism, two premises and a conclusion linked by three terms.
vocabulary.example: 'All mammals are animals; all dogs are mammals; so all dogs are animals' is a classic syllogism.

vocabulary.definition: A statement offered as a starting point or reason in an argument, from which the conclusion is drawn.
vocabulary.example: If you doubt the conclusion of a valid argument, you must reject at least one premise.

vocabulary.definition: In a categorical syllogism, the term that appears in both premises but not in the conclusion, linking the other two terms.
vocabulary.example: In 'All humans are mortal; all Greeks are humans; so all Greeks are mortal', the middle term is 'humans'.

vocabulary.definition: The property of an argument whose conclusion must be true if its premises are true; it depends on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are actually true.
vocabulary.example: 'All fish fly; all sharks are fish; so all sharks fly' has validity even though its conclusion is false.

vocabulary.definition: The property of an argument that is both valid and has all true premises, which guarantees a true conclusion.
vocabulary.example: To show an argument lacks soundness, you can either deny a premise or show the reasoning is invalid.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that a statement and its denial cannot both be true at the same time and in the same respect; Aristotle called it the firmest of all principles.
vocabulary.example: By the law of non-contradiction, the door cannot be both fully open and not fully open at the same moment.

vocabulary.definition: Reasoning from particular observed cases to a general conclusion; useful and necessary, but never logically guaranteed.
vocabulary.example: Concluding that all swans are white after seeing thousands of white swans was an induction that turned out to be false.

thinkingExercise.title: Argument Repair Shop
thinkingExercise.prompt: Practice using Aristotle's tools on arguments from everyday life.
steps: Find or invent three short arguments from news, advertising or conversation (for example, 'All successful people get up early; I get up early; so I will be successful'). Write each one out as clearly separated premises and a conclusion.
For each, ask the validity question: if the premises were true, would the conclusion have to be true? If not, try to draw circles to show why the bridge (the middle term) fails.
For each, ask the truth question: are the premises actually true? Mark any you doubt.
Choose one argument and repair it: rewrite it so that it is both valid and, as far as you can tell, sound. Notice what you had to add or weaken.

summary: Aristotle founded formal logic; his logical works, collected as the Organon ('tool'), were meant as the instrument for all other inquiry.
A categorical syllogism has two premises and a conclusion built from three terms; the middle term links the major and minor terms.
There are four kinds of categorical statement (A, E, I, O); validity depends on form, so valid patterns like Barbara work for any subject matter.
Validity is not truth: a valid argument can have a false conclusion, and a sound argument is valid with all premises true.
Aristotle called the law of non-contradiction the firmest principle; it cannot be proved, but anyone who denies it relies on it, and he also defended the law of excluded middle.

Deduction gives necessity from general premises; induction gets general premises from particulars. Aristotle's logic dominated for two thousand years until the Stoics' insights were revived and Frege created modern logic.

quiz.question: What does 'Organon', the name given to Aristotle's logical works, mean?
quiz.explanation: Organon means tool or instrument, reflecting the view that logic is the instrument needed for all other knowledge.

quiz.question: In the syllogism 'All birds have feathers; all penguins are birds; therefore all penguins have feathers', what is the middle term?
quiz.explanation: 'Birds' appears in both premises but not in the conclusion; it links penguins to feathers.

quiz.question: A valid argument always has a true conclusion.
quiz.explanation: A valid argument guarantees a true conclusion only if its premises are true. Valid arguments with false premises can have false conclusions.

quiz.question: Which statement is an 'O' type (particular negative) statement?
quiz.explanation: 'Some S are not P' is the O form. The others are A, E and I statements respectively.

quiz.question: What makes an argument 'sound'?
options: It is valid and all of its premises are true
It is persuasive to most listeners
quiz.explanation: Soundness combines valid form with true premises, which together guarantee a true conclusion.

quiz.question: What is wrong with the argument 'All cats are mammals; all dogs are mammals; therefore all cats are dogs'?
options: One of its premises is false
Its conclusion is a universal statement
The middle term never covers the whole class of mammals, so it does not link cats to dogs
quiz.explanation: Both premises are true, but they only place cats and dogs somewhere inside the mammal circle, so no conclusion about cats and dogs follows. The form is invalid.

quiz.question: Aristotle claimed that the law of non-contradiction can be proved from more basic principles.
quiz.explanation: He said it is the firmest principle and cannot be proved, since any proof would assume it; instead he showed that anyone who denies it refutes himself by speaking meaningfully.

quiz.question: A doctor sees that a medicine helped hundreds of patients and concludes it will generally help patients with that illness. What kind of reasoning is this?
quiz.explanation: Reasoning from many particular cases to a general rule is induction. It is useful but never guaranteed, since the next case might differ.

quiz.question: Which pair of statements are contradictories, so that exactly one must be true?
options: 'All swans are white' and 'Some swans are white'
'Some swans are white' and 'Some swans are not white'
'All swans are white' and 'Some swans are not white'
'No swans are white' and 'All swans are black'
quiz.explanation: A and O statements with the same terms contradict each other: if not all swans are white, then some swans are not white, and vice versa.

quiz.question: Immanuel Kant believed logic had made little or no real progress since Aristotle, but later developments such as Frege's logic showed that formal logic could go far beyond the syllogism.
quiz.explanation: Kant thought Aristotle's logic seemed complete; Frege's 1879 logic, building on ideas the Stoics had partly anticipated, transformed the field.

goDeeper.body:
Is the law of excluded middle really universal? Aristotle himself raised a famous problem in chapter 9 of *On Interpretation*: the sea battle. Either there will be a sea battle tomorrow or there will not. But if one of those statements is *already* true today, isn't the future already fixed, so that nothing we do matters? Aristotle's own answer is still debated. Many read him as saying that statements about future contingent events are not yet true or false, though the disjunction 'either there will be a battle or not' is necessarily true. This puzzle connects logic to the problem of free will, which returns with Augustine (Day 30).

In the twentieth century, logicians took these doubts further. The Dutch mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer founded **intuitionism**, which rejects excluded middle in mathematics: a statement counts as true only if we can construct a proof of it, so some statements may be neither proved nor disproved. Even more radically, the philosopher Graham Priest has defended **dialetheism**, the view that some contradictions are true, for example the liar sentence 'This sentence is false.' Paraconsistent logics are designed so that a contradiction in a database or theory does not make everything follow from it. Most philosophers still side with Aristotle on non-contradiction, but these debates show that even the 'laws of thought' can be questioned.

Finally, historians now appreciate that Aristotle had a rival. The Stoic Chrysippus (Day 25) developed a sophisticated logic of propositions connected by 'if', 'and' and 'or', closer in spirit to modern logic. For centuries it was overshadowed and largely lost, and its importance was only fully recognized in the twentieth century.

readings.title: Prior Analytics, Book I, chapters 1–7
readings.author: Aristotle (trans. Robin Smith)
readings.note: Where Aristotle defines the syllogism and works through the valid forms of the first three figures; demanding but foundational.

readings.title: Metaphysics, Book IV (Gamma), chapters 3–4
readings.author: Aristotle (trans. W. D. Ross or C. D. C. Reeve)
readings.note: Aristotle's defense of the law of non-contradiction, including the jokes about plants and walking into wells.

readings.title: Logic: A Very Short Introduction
readings.author: Graham Priest
readings.note: A lively introduction to modern logic by a leading logician who himself questions the law of non-contradiction.

readings.title: Aristotle: A Very Short Introduction
readings.author: Jonathan Barnes
readings.note: Its chapters on logic and science explain the syllogism and its role in Aristotle's picture of knowledge.

questions: Can you think of a situation where it seems that a statement and its denial are both true? Is it a real contradiction, or does it involve different times, respects or senses?
If induction can never be logically guaranteed, why is it rational to rely on it, for example in medicine or engineering?
Is it a strength or a weakness of formal logic that it ignores content and looks only at form?
